situation.p1: The regime that ruled Indonesia for 32 years did not fall so much as it rotted from within, gutted in the span of ten months by the §FAsian Financial Crisis§! that swept out of Bangkok in July 1997. By the spring of 1998, campus sit-ins had spilled into the avenues of the capital. In the late afternoon of May 12, 1998, as thousands of students at Trisakti University in Grogol retreated back inside their campus gates after being blocked from marching on parliament, security forces opened fire from the street and the overpass above with live ammunition. §FFour students were shot dead§! on their own campus grounds: Elang Mulia Lesmana, Hery Hertanto, Hafidin Royan, and Hendriawan Sie. None of them were armed; all four were struck in the head, throat, or chest by live rounds.
situation.p2: For the next three days, from May 13 to May 15, Jakarta and Surakarta burned, following days of violent unrest that had already torn through Medan. Some mobs formed spontaneously in the slums, while others—men with military-style crewcuts trucked in from the outskirts—operated with chilling coordination. Rioters looted and torched more than 4,000 commercial buildings, banks, and homes, overwhelmingly targeting ethnic Chinese-Indonesians who had been scapegoated by regime figures and resented for decades as the visible face of New Order cronyism. Over 1,180 people perished in Jakarta alone, hundreds of them trapped and burned alive inside shuttered department stores like Klender's Yogya Plaza as exits were barred from the outside. As the Joint Fact-Finding Team (TGPF) and Father Sandyawan Sumardi's volunteer network later documented, dozens of Chinese-Indonesian women and girls were systematically hunted down and gang-raped in their homes and shophouses across Glodok, Pluit, and Jatinegara; some were mutilated or thrown into the flames afterward, and §Fnot a single perpetrator was ever convicted.§! By May 18, tens of thousands of students had scaled the gates and green-domed roof of the MPR/DPR complex in Senayan, joined by longtime regime loyalist and House Speaker Harmoko in demanding Suharto's resignation. Abandoned on the night of May 20 by fourteen economic ministers led by Ginandjar Kartasasmita, Suharto stepped before the cameras in Merdeka Palace at 9:05 a.m. on May 21, 1998, and resigned. Minutes later, in the palace's Credentials Room before Chief Justice Sarwata, you—Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie, a German-trained aerospace engineer and Suharto's lifelong protégé—took the oath as third President of the Republic, inheriting a state most foreign chancellories doubted would survive the month.
situation.p3: You took the helm of a banking system in cardiac arrest and a currency in freefall. The rupiah, which had traded at 2,450 to the US dollar in June 1997, had plunged to nearly 16,800 by mid-June 1998—an 85% collapse that rendered the private sector's $80 billion in unhedged foreign debt unpayable overnight, forced the newly created Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) to take over dozens of bleeding banks, and drove Jakarta back to the §IIMF§! for successive, humiliating bailout revisions. Real GDP contracted by 13.1% in 1998, while annual inflation tore past 77% and food prices more than doubled. Rice, cooking oil, sugar, and basic medicine climbed out of reach as Bulog's supply lines frayed, shoving more than twenty million Indonesians back below the poverty line inside a single calendar year.
situation.p4: Yet in the thirteen months since that morning at Merdeka Palace—beginning with your dismissal of Suharto's son-in-law, Lt. Gen. Prabowo Subianto, from the command of Kostrad on May 22 as armed troops maneuvered near your Kuningan residence—your caretaker administration has dismantled pillars of the New Order at a breakneck pace. You opened the gates of Cipinang Prison for political detainees like Sri Bintang Pamungkas and Muchtar Pakpahan, ratified ILO conventions ending the state monopoly over labor unions, and separated the National Police from the military chain of command. Through Information Minister Yunus Yosfiah, you abolished the dreaded SIUPP press-licensing regime that had allowed ministers to ban newspapers with a phone call, and pushed through the January 1999 Political Laws allowing 48 parties to contest the country's first free general election since 1955. You lifted the military's decade-long Daerah Operasi Militer (DOM) status in Aceh, stood at the Baiturrahman Grand Mosque in Banda Aceh on March 26, 1999, to apologize in person for decades of state abuses, and in January 1999 stunned the world—and your own generals—by offering East Timor a UN-supervised ballot between special autonomy and outright independence.
situation.p5: It is now June 1999. On June 7, more than 105 million Indonesians cast their ballots in a peaceful national election, and the returns are unforgiving. §PMegawati Sukarnoputri's PDI-P§! has surged to first place with 33.7% of the popular vote and 153 seats in the DPR, while her red-shirted supporters fill the roundabouts of Jakarta demanding that the daughter of Sukarno take the presidency immediately. Your own party, Golkar, has fallen to second place with 22.4% (120 seats)—and its Jakarta machine at DPP Slipi under Chairman Akbar Tandjung is already hedging its bets, deeply divided between your Eastern Indonesian 'Iramasuka' loyalists and old-guard pragmatists looking to save themselves. Though tight monetary policy and IMF disbursements have pulled the rupiah back to between 6,700 and 7,500 to the dollar, the recovery remains brittle, hostage to every rumor out of Senayan and every scandal in the recapitalized banks.
situation.p6: Worse still, the archipelago's peripheries are bleeding. In §XAceh§!, the goodwill of your March apology evaporated on May 3 when soldiers opened fire on demonstrators at the Simpang KKA crossroads in North Aceh, killing dozens and driving a new generation into the ranks of the Free Aceh Movement (GAM). In §XEast Timor§!, despite the May 5 New York Agreement establishing the UNAMET mission, pro-integration militias like Eurico Guterres's Aitarak and Besi Merah Putih—armed and sheltered by local Kodam IX/Udayana and special forces officers—are waging a campaign of intimidation ahead of the August 30 Popular Consultation, having already slaughtered civilians inside the Liquiçá church complex in April. Sectarian bloodshed between Christians and Muslims has turned Ambon and the Maluku islands into a warzone since January, while in Cilangkap, General Wiranto's officer corps watches Bina Graha with cold suspicion, fearful that a civilian president without an electoral base of his own will trade away the armed forces' 38 reserved parliamentary seats, their territorial command structure, and their impunity for 1998 just to buy another five years in the palace.
situation.p7: You have barely four months left. In October 1999, all 700 delegates of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR)—462 elected legislators, 135 provincial delegates, 65 functional group representatives, and 38 military appointees—will convene in Senayan to hear and vote by secret ballot on your Pidato Pertanggungjawaban. Only if that accountability report is accepted can your name even stand for the presidency. The banyan tree that shaded and strangled Indonesian politics for thirty-two years is hollowing out, its roots still tangled through every ministry, barracks, and courtroom in the Republic. What grows in its place—and whether your presidency survives the harvest—will be decided on the floor of Senayan.
bio.habibie.title: B.J. Habibie
bio.habibie.p1: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie was born on June 25, 1936, in the port town of Parepare, South Sulawesi, the fourth of eight children born to Alwi Abdul Jalil Habibie, an agricultural official of Gorontalese descent, and R.A. Tuti Marini Puspowardojo, a Javanese noblewoman from Yogyakarta. On September 3, 1950, when Habibie—"Rudy" to his family—was just fourteen, his father suffered a fatal heart attack during evening prayers. Determined that her children receive a modern education, his widowed mother moved the family to Bandung and sold off family property to fund his studies. After a year studying mechanical engineering at the Bandung Institute of Technology (ITB) in 1954, Habibie traveled to West Germany in 1955 to study aerospace engineering at the Rheinisch-Westfälische Technische Hochschule (RWTH) in Aachen, initially financed directly by his mother before his academic record earned him a state scholarship from Jakarta.
bio.habibie.p2: Surviving harsh European winters and a bout of tuberculosis that nearly killed him, Habibie earned his Diplom-Ingenieur in 1960, married his high-school contemporary Hasri Ainun Besari in 1962, and completed his Doktor-Ingenieur in 1965 with the highest distinction, summa cum laude, defending a dissertation on thermoelastic stress in supersonic flight. Joining Hamburger Flugzeugbau—which merged into the West German aerospace giant Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm (MBB) in 1969—he rose to become Vice President for Applied Technology, the highest post held by a foreign national in the German aviation industry. There he formulated mathematical methods for calculating metal fatigue and crack propagation down to the atomic lattice on the wings of the Airbus A300 and NATO transport aircraft, earning the lifelong moniker 'Mr. Crack.' In December 1973, President Suharto dispatched Pertamina chief Ibnu Sutowo to Dusseldorf to summon Habibie home to spearhead Indonesia's industrial modernization. Returning to Jakarta in 1974, Habibie established the Agency for the Assessment and Application of Technology (BPPT) and, in 1976, founded the state aircraft manufacturer PT Industri Pesawat Terbang Nurtanio—later Nusantara (IPTN)—in Bandung.
bio.habibie.p3: From March 1978 to March 1998, Habibie served across five consecutive cabinets as State Minister of Research and Technology (Menristek) and head of the Strategic Industries Management Agency (BPIS), presiding over shipyards, munitions plants, steelworks, and the Batam industrial zone. Championed by Suharto as a surrogate son, Habibie clashed repeatedly with Berkeley-trained finance technocrats over state subsidies for his crowning ambition: the indigenous, fly-by-wire N-250 Gatotkaca turboprop, whose maiden flight on August 10, 1995, became the centerpiece of the Republic's fiftieth independence anniversary. In December 1990, with Suharto's blessing, he became founding chairman of the Association of Indonesian Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI), transforming a network of modernist Muslim scholars and bureaucrats into a formidable counterweight to the secular-nationalist military brass inside Golkar. When Suharto tapped him as the nation's seventh Vice President in March 1998 at the height of the Asian Financial Crisis, foreign currency markets recoiled at his reputation for big-ticket industrial spending. Ten weeks later—after Suharto spurned him on the eve of stepping down—Habibie was sworn in as President at Merdeka Palace on the morning of May 21, 1998, tasked with dismantling from within the authoritarian edifice that had sheltered his entire career, stabilizing a shattered economy, and fighting for legitimacy before a parliament that viewed him as an accidental caretaker.
